headline.en_html: Nvidia Opens Investigation Into Jensen Huang's Relationship With Chinese Spy
headline.zh: 千亿帝国掌舵人的私密丑闻：黄仁勋承认出轨，对方被美情报部门认定为间谍

paragraphs.en_html: Nvidia said on Sunday that it was opening an investigation into Jensen Huang, its chief executive and co-founder, after he acknowledged to the company’s board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy. In a message to the company, Mr. Huang apologized. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The relationship and affair are a rare misstep for Mr. Huang. Over the past three years, he could do no wrong. His chipmaker, which makes the technology to build artificial intelligence, grew into one of the world’s most valuable companies and the engine of the data center boom powering the U.S. economy. He started being followed by autograph-seeking throngs at events. And his black leather jackets, which he wears daily, became collectors’ items. Mr. Huang has credited his wife, Lori, whom he married in 1985, with making it possible for him to build the company.

Public scrutiny of Mr. Huang’s ties with Ms. Huang began after The New York Times first reported last month that American intelligence agencies had discovered that Mr. Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, who U.S. officials concluded was gathering intelligence for Beijing. The chip buyer was Ms. Huang or Huang Le, whose biography said she worked in China as a TV reporter before becoming a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company that had become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia.

Megaspeed was formed in 2023, when a Chinese online gaming company split off its Singaporean subsidiary. Megaspeed is among the firms in Southeast Asia that buy chips to build data centers and then rent their computing power to companies in China. Megaspeed is essentially a middle man. Megaspeed’s sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of advanced AI equipment containing Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records obtained from ImportGenius, a trade platform. It was an exceptional amount of money for a small, obscure company.

The U.S. government has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visited its data center in Malaysia and found the site to be suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, suggesting it was being shipped in or out rather than installed there. Investigators suspect that some Nvidia chips acquired by Megaspeed are also finding their way illegally into China. Singapore has conducted its own investigation into Megaspeed. In 2025, Singaporean authorities brought Alice Huang in for questioning, but subsequently released her.

As Megaspeed’s chip purchases rolled in, Mr. Huang and Ms. Huang began spending time together. Their relationship became a preoccupation in Washington, where officials were already alarmed by the large volume of Megaspeed’s purchases. Nvidia and Mr. Huang initially said there was nothing problematic or unusual about his relationship with Ms. Huang. In an interview with Bloomberg News last month, he said that his interactions with Ms. Huang had been “related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual.”

The U.S. government, which had been investigating Megaspeed for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China, began its surveillance of Ms. Huang more than a year ago. In the course of the surveillance, they found that she was in communication with a U.S. citizen who was identified as Mr. Huang. Officials who had seen that intelligence said they were certain the relationship was romantic. That undercut Nvidia’s original misleading statements to The Times and others over the course of the last year about the nature of Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang.

As news about the U.S. surveillance of Ms. Huang broke, Mr. Huang’s room to maneuver all but disappeared. Congress wanted him to testify, probably under oath, and reporting on the surveillance raised the possibility that U.S. intelligence knew the nature of his relationship with Ms. Huang. There was also pressure on Nvidia’s board. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that “the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Mr. Huang, 63, will continue to lead the company during the investigation, the board said. He also received public support from President Trump. Asked by reporters whether he would bring Mr. Huang on his upcoming trip to China, Mr. Trump said, “I’d certainly take him.” He also described Mr. Huang as “an honorable guy.” As a co-founder, Mr. Huang has set up a unique structure at Nvidia where he dictates all aspects of its business while overseeing some 60 people who directly report to him. “Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” Mr. Rizzo said. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as C.E.O. without interruption.” Many questions about the situation remain unanswered, at least publicly.

sources_note: 依据美国《纽约时报》（The New York Times）2026-11-10 报道。
